checks.prompt: Before comparing two models on a benchmark, what single measurement most cheaply tells you which comparisons are worth making at all?
options: Run the SAME model twice and look at the difference — that is your noise floor
Measure how long the evaluation takes, to budget for repeats
Check that both models were evaluated on the same items
checks.explanation: Any model comparison smaller than the difference between two runs of one model is not evidence of anything. It costs one extra eval run and is skipped almost universally.

checks.prompt: Evals are framed as polling in this notebook. Explain what the 1/sqrt(n) rule implies for benchmark size, and why the polling analogy breaks down in a way that is favourable to evals.
checks.expected: A correct answer must explain that the margin of error shrinks as 1/sqrt(n), so HALVING the error bar requires FOUR TIMES the items — which is why a small benchmark cannot resolve small differences no matter how carefully it is built. It must then identify the favourable break in the analogy: a pollster cannot re-interview the same person under identical conditions, but you CAN re-run a model, which gives a direct measurement of generation/run-to-run noise that pollsters cannot obtain. Noting that this measurement is exactly the noise floor, and is rarely taken, is a plus.
checks.explanation: Quadratic cost in precision is the fact that governs benchmark design; free re-measurement is the advantage evals have over polls and mostly waste.

checks.prompt: Why is McNemar's test the right significance test for comparing two models on a benchmark?
options: Both models answer the same items, so the comparison is paired, and McNemar's test uses only the items where they disagree
It is the only test that works for binary outcomes
It corrects for the multiple comparisons introduced by testing many benchmarks
It does not assume the items are independent, unlike the two-proportion z-test
checks.explanation: Items both models got right, or both got wrong, carry no information about which is better but do inflate the variance of an unpaired estimate. Conditioning on the disagreements is what buys the extra power.

checks.prompt: Write `wilson_interval(k, n, z=1.96)` returning a (low, high) tuple for the Wilson score confidence interval of a proportion k/n. Return (0.0, 1.0) when n is 0, and clamp the result into [0, 1]. Standard library only.
checks.test:
lo, hi = wilson_interval(0, 50)
assert lo == 0.0 and hi > 0.0, 'k=0 must still have positive width'
lo, hi = wilson_interval(20, 20)
assert hi == 1.0 and lo < 1.0, 'k=n must still have positive width'
lo, hi = wilson_interval(75, 100)
assert lo < 0.75 < hi, 'interval must contain the point estimate'
w_small = wilson_interval(150, 200)
w_big = wilson_interval(1500, 2000)
assert (w_big[1]-w_big[0]) < (w_small[1]-w_small[0]), 'more data -> tighter'
for k, n in [(1, 30), (29, 30), (0, 10), (10, 10)]:
    lo, hi = wilson_interval(k, n)
    assert 0.0 <= lo <= hi <= 1.0, (k, n, lo, hi)
assert wilson_interval(5, 0) == (0.0, 1.0)
checks.explanation: The normal-approximation ('Wald') interval runs past 100% at extreme proportions and collapses to zero width at k=0 or k=n. Wilson stays valid, and it is four lines.

checks.prompt: You evaluate a new training recipe on 20 benchmarks and two show significant improvement at p < 0.05. What is the problem?
options: With 20 independent tests at the 5% level you expect about one false positive even if nothing changed — correct for the number of tests, or pre-register a primary metric
Two out of twenty is too few to establish an effect; you need a majority to improve
p < 0.05 is too lenient a threshold for machine learning experiments generally
The benchmarks are not independent, so the p-values cannot be combined
checks.explanation: The notebook's simulation finds at least one 'significant' result in most sweeps where nothing was different. Holm-Bonferroni or a pre-registered primary metric are the fixes.

checks.prompt: Your benchmark groups twenty questions per reading passage. Explain why naive confidence intervals will be too narrow, and what to do instead.
checks.expected: A correct answer must explain that items sharing a passage are NOT INDEPENDENT — their outcomes are correlated, because a model that understands (or misreads) the passage tends to get the whole group right or wrong together — so the effective sample size is closer to the number of PASSAGES than the number of questions. A standard binomial or Wilson interval assumes independence and therefore understates the uncertainty. It must recommend accounting for the clustering: a CLUSTER BOOTSTRAP that resamples whole passages rather than individual questions (or an equivalent clustered standard error).
checks.explanation: Twenty questions about one passage are far closer to one observation than to twenty, and the interval must reflect that.
